title: Azure deployment and network boundaries
summary: A classic workspace resource with a locked managed group, two supported network patterns, two authorization chains and one query path: who owns each boundary on Azure, and how a denied request differs from an unreachable one.
outcomes: Place the tenant, subscription, workspace resource, managed resource group, control plane and both compute planes, and say which of them Cinderline can change.
Compare the default managed VNet with VNet injection by who creates, changes and diagnoses each network piece, including routes, NSG rules and private endpoints.
Keep application access (Entra identity and Unity Catalog privileges) separate from storage access (access connector managed identity, Azure data role and storage network rules).
Run ordered diagnoses for a denied and an unreachable request, assemble an evidence checklist and list what differs from AWS without provisioning anything.
startingAssumptions: The platform module separates account, workspace, catalog, compute and storage.
The cloud bridge and the trust-boundary lesson have covered DNS, routing, identity and authorization in general terms.
editorialRationale: Azure deployment teaching fails when it relabels an AWS picture, so the module starts from the objects Azure itself creates, a classic workspace resource with a locked managed resource group and Entra identities, then compares the two supported network patterns, follows egress, legacy keys, the access connector and private connectivity as separate boundaries, keeps application access apart from storage access, and ends with two ordered diagnoses, an evidence checklist and an explicit list of AWS differences that a later three-cloud lab can align. Tier, region and preview status stay verification items throughout.

claims.description: The control plane, including the web application, runs in the Azure Databricks account; classic compute runs in the customer's Azure subscription; serverless compute runs in the Azure Databricks account within a network boundary for the workspace; workspace storage holds workspace file system and system data, separate from Unity Catalog tables and volumes.

claims.description: Creating a classic Azure Databricks workspace provisions a managed resource group holding the resources the workspace needs, such as virtual machines, storage accounts and networking components; the creating user becomes a workspace admin; creation can take minutes to hours; the Microsoft.Databricks API's Serverless compute mode does not accept a managed resource group.
claims.context: Workspace resource and managed resource group on Azure.

claims.description: Deny assignments, created and managed by Azure, block resource actions even when a role assignment grants them; Azure Databricks places a system deny assignment on its managed resource group, removed only when the workspace is deleted, so tags belong on the workspace resource.
claims.context: The Databricks-specific behaviour comes from a Microsoft Q&A answer and is verified on the current workspace before quoting it in a review.

claims.description: A Microsoft Entra ID Global Administrator establishes the Databricks account's first account admin; the SCIM provisioning connector cannot sync nested groups or Entra service principals; automatic identity management syncs users, groups, memberships, nested groups and service principals and is documented as enabled by default for accounts created after August 1, 2025.
claims.context: Azure Databricks identities from Microsoft Entra ID; confirm the account's provisioning method.

claims.description: Entra security principals that can hold Azure roles are users, groups, application service principals and managed identities; a managed identity's service principal has no application object and cannot be modified directly; a system-assigned identity shares its resource's lifecycle, a user-assigned one has its own.
claims.context: Microsoft Entra and Azure RBAC; applies to any Azure resource, not only Databricks.

claims.description: VNet injection uses two dedicated subnets, host and container, delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces and not shared with other workspaces or resources, in a /16 to /24 VNet with subnets no smaller than /26; each node takes one address in each subnet and Azure reserves five per subnet; Databricks provisions and manages the required NSG rules through the delegation; a NAT gateway on both subnets is recommended for stable egress.
claims.context: Classic compute plane on Azure; exact ranges and rules are read from the current page.

claims.description: With secure cluster connectivity, classic nodes have no public IP addresses and the VNet has no open ports; each cluster connects outbound on port 443 to the control plane's relay over the Microsoft backbone; it is enabled automatically for portal and ARM deployments; the default VNet gets a NAT gateway from Databricks, while an injected workspace should have a stable egress IP.
claims.context: Azure classic compute plane.

claims.description: An injected workspace needs a user-defined route for every type of outbound connection; Databricks recommends service tags over IP addresses; the AzureDatabricks tag covers the control plane, secure cluster connectivity relay and web application, the Storage tag artifact and log Blob storage, and the EventHub tag logging.
claims.context: User-defined routes for Azure Databricks; the destination list changes.

claims.description: Azure chooses a route by longest prefix match; next hop types include Virtual network, Internet, None and Virtual appliance, and a 0.0.0.0/0 route to a virtual appliance lets it inspect traffic; Internet-bound traffic to Azure services travels the Azure backbone; service tags can be route prefixes, up to 25 such routes per table; the effective routes of a virtual machine network interface combine default, custom and propagated routes and can be viewed to diagnose routing.
claims.context: Azure Virtual Network routing; limits change.

claims.description: For API versions released after March 31, 2026, subnets in new virtual networks are private by default, so virtual machines need an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway or a route to a firewall; existing virtual networks are unchanged.
claims.context: Azure default outbound access retirement; check each subnet's setting.

claims.description: Direct access to ADLS Gen2 outside Unity Catalog uses the abfss driver with an Entra service principal's OAuth credentials, a storage account key or a SAS token; Shared Key grants access to every resource in the account, service and account SAS tokens are signed with the account key, SAS generation cannot be audited, and disallowing Shared Key rejects key-authorized requests while Entra-authorized ones continue.
claims.context: Contrast case; read the current pages for which methods are legacy.

claims.description: The ABFS driver addresses Data Lake Storage as abfs[s]://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/path, abfss meaning TLS, on an account with hierarchical namespace enabled; Unity Catalog external locations use the same abfss path form.
claims.context: Azure Storage and Azure Databricks path format.

claims.description: An access connector for Azure Databricks is a first-party Azure resource carrying a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity; that identity is granted a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor; a storage credential names the connector's resource ID and an external location binds an abfss path to the credential; a managed identity needs no secret rotation and can reach storage protected by network rules, unlike a service principal; Unity Catalog checks access to the credential or location before authenticating to Azure.
claims.context: Unity Catalog storage access on Azure; steps and role choices are on the current pages.

claims.description: Storage firewall rules admit traffic to an account's public endpoint by virtual network, IP, resource instance or trusted-service exception; allowed sources must still be authorized; a disallowed subnet receives a 403; a resource instance rule admits the endpoint, not the data, which needs a role for the resource's managed identity; Azure Databricks access connectors are admitted by managed identity.
claims.context: Azure Storage network security; private endpoints are configured separately.

claims.description: Creating a storage account grants no data access through Entra; data roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Contributor are assigned explicitly at subscription, resource group, account or container scope, and changes can take up to ten minutes to apply.
claims.context: Azure RBAC for blob and Data Lake data.

claims.description: Azure Databricks supports three independently enabled Private Link types: inbound from users through databricks_ui_api and browser_authentication endpoints in a transit VNet, classic from clusters through a databricks_ui_api endpoint in the workspace VNet, which requires the Premium plan and VNet injection, and outbound from serverless compute; compute must resolve the workspace URL to the endpoint's private IP through privatelink.azuredatabricks.net linked to its VNet or DNS forwarding.
claims.context: Azure Private Link with Azure Databricks; configuration details change.

claims.description: Public DNS returns a CNAME into a privatelink name that a linked Private DNS zone can answer with a private endpoint's IP; the zones are privatelink.azuredatabricks.net for Azure Databricks, privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net for the ADLS dfs sub-resource and privatelink.blob.core.windows.net for blob; DNS resolution and access control are independent, and a resource with public access disabled rejects connections whatever DNS says.
claims.context: Azure Private Endpoint DNS, commercial cloud.

claims.description: A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP from the VNet; its connection is Approved, Pending, Rejected or Disconnected, only Approved endpoints carry traffic, and a manual request waits for the resource owner's approval; each storage sub-resource needs its own endpoint.
claims.context: Azure Private Link.

claims.description: Network connectivity configurations are account-level regional objects attached to workspaces; without a private endpoint, serverless reaches Azure storage through service endpoints from stable subnets and other resources from NAT IPs; a private endpoint rule makes Databricks request an endpoint that the resource owner must approve, and it is effective only when ESTABLISHED, expiring if not approved within 14 days; changes usually propagate within ten minutes and can take up to 24 hours.
claims.context: Azure serverless compute plane; availability, limits and charges vary.

claims.description: Serverless egress control applies account-level network policies, one per workspace at a time, that set the network access mode for serverless workloads; account admins manage them from the account console; the workspace must be on the Premium tier; most changes refresh within ten minutes and mode or enforcement changes can take up to 24 hours.
claims.context: Azure serverless egress control; regional availability is verified on the current page.

claims.description: The workspace storage account in the managed resource group holds workspace system data and the DBFS root; enabling its firewall support blocks public access, Databricks reaches it through an access connector associated with the workspace, serverless must use service or private endpoints, and the trusted-services setting admits any Azure Databricks access connector in the same tenant.
claims.context: Workspace storage account firewall on Azure; availability and steps are verified on the current page.

claims.description: Azure Databricks customer-managed keys come from Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM for managed disks (classic compute only), managed services (control-plane data) and the DBFS root (not additional mounts); the DBFS root Key Vault needs soft delete and purge protection.
claims.context: Azure Key Vault with Azure Databricks; a customer's own data lake encryption is outside these features.

claims.description: The Databricks SDK turns an Azure login redirect carrying a private-link-validation-error into PrivateLinkValidationError, a subclass of PermissionDenied whose message says the workspace has Azure Private Link enabled and is not accessible from the current network.
claims.context: Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 behaviour; the portal's own wording may differ.

claims.description: When a VNet uses a Private DNS zone for a resource type, it resolves public resources of that type only if they have no private endpoint connections; otherwise the zone answers NXDOMAIN unless fallback to internet or another DNS configuration is added.
claims.context: Azure Private Endpoint DNS caution.

concepts.definition: The resource group Azure provisions with a classic Databricks workspace resource to hold its storage account, networking components and cluster virtual machines, protected by a system deny assignment.
concepts.example: rg-dbw-prod-managed holds the workspace storage account and default VNet of dbw-cinderline-prod; Cinderline can read it but not edit it.

concepts.definition: A user, group, service principal or managed identity held in the Microsoft Entra tenant, which Databricks can sync as an account identity and Azure can assign roles to.

concepts.definition: An Entra service principal that Azure creates for a resource, with no application object and no credential anyone manages, used to obtain tokens for that resource.

concepts.definition: The ordered sequence of components one request crosses, each boundary with its own owner, control and way of failing.
concepts.example: Browser and Entra sign-in to the workspace URL; relay to cluster; Unity Catalog; cluster to stcinderlinelake over abfss.

concepts.definition: One of the two supported ways a classic workspace's network is provided on Azure: created by Databricks in the managed resource group, or injected into a VNet the customer owns.

concepts.definition: A custom route on the workspace subnets that sends a class of outbound traffic to a chosen next hop, selected by longest prefix match and writable with service tags.

concepts.definition: Storage authorization by the account key or by tokens signed with it, which authorize the bearer for the account or the token's scope rather than a named identity.
concepts.example: A legacy notebook sets fs.azure.account.key for stcinderlinelake, and the storage account cannot tell who ran it.

concepts.definition: The Azure resource whose managed identity Unity Catalog uses to reach a storage account, registered as a storage credential and bound to paths by external locations.
concepts.example: ac-cinderline-uc backs cinderline_lake_cred; cinderline_quality binds abfss://quality@stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net/accepted.

concepts.definition: The Azure Blob File System driver's address form, abfss://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/path, where abfss means the driver over TLS against the account's dfs endpoint.
concepts.example: abfss://quality@stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net/accepted names container quality, account stcinderlinelake and path accepted.

concepts.definition: The split between whether a principal may query through Databricks, decided by Unity Catalog, and whether Databricks may reach the files, decided by Azure roles and network rules on the credential's identity.
concepts.example: Analysts hold SELECT and no Azure role; the connector's identity holds a data role and no catalog grant.

concepts.definition: The storage account settings that admit or refuse traffic to its public endpoint by network source, independently of authorization: virtual network, IP, resource instance and trusted-service rules.
concepts.example: stcinderlinesup, set to selected networks, admits the connector's resource instance and the NCC subnets; the office network receives a 403.

concepts.definition: One of three independently enabled private connections for Azure Databricks: users to workspaces, classic compute to the control plane, and serverless compute to customer resources.
concepts.example: pe-dbw-sec-fe in the transit VNet serves analysts; pe-dbw-sec-be in vnet-cinderline-data serves clusters.

concepts.definition: An Azure DNS zone, linked to chosen VNets, that answers a privatelink name with a private endpoint's address for those networks only.
concepts.example: privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net linked to vnet-cinderline-data answers 10.20.2.5 for stcinderlinelake.

concepts.definition: An account-level, regional Databricks object attached to workspaces that gives serverless compute stable subnets or approved private endpoints to customer resources.
concepts.example: ncc-cinderline holds a dfs rule for stcinderlinelake that stayed PENDING until the storage owner approved it.

concepts.definition: The specific control that refused a request that did arrive: a Unity Catalog privilege, an Azure data role or a storage network rule.
concepts.example: PERMISSION_DENIED names the catalog; a storage 403 after the catalog agreed points at the role or the network rules.

concepts.definition: The step at which a request never arrived: the DNS answer, the endpoint's approval, the route's next hop, the NSG or the firewall.
concepts.example: The cluster resolved stcinderlinelake to a public address because the dfs zone was linked to the hub only.

concepts.definition: A table naming, for each boundary, what to capture, which Azure or Databricks object holds it and what it does not prove.
concepts.example: A role assignment export proves a permission and nothing about a route; a name lookup proves resolution, not approval.

concepts.definition: An explicit list of where Azure's deployment boundaries sit differently from AWS's, used to stop a runbook being translated term for term.
concepts.example: Delegated subnets with Databricks-managed NSG rules replace a customer VPC security group; a role assignment replaces a trust policy.

concepts.definition: The documented option that blocks public network access to the workspace storage account in the managed resource group and admits Databricks through an access connector associated with the workspace.
concepts.example: After enabling it, the workspace storage account of dbw-cinderline-sec answers only authorized resources, serverless through service or private endpoints.

concepts.definition: An account-level policy, one per workspace at a time, that sets the network access mode for outbound connections from serverless compute.
concepts.example: Cinderline would attach a restricted policy to dbw-cinderline-sec only after confirming availability for its region.

concepts.definition: Azure's change under which subnets of VNets created with API versions released after March 31, 2026 have no default outbound access unless configured otherwise, so virtual machines need an explicit outbound method.
concepts.example: In a new vnet-cinderline-data with private subnets, the Internet-next-hop service-tag routes of rt-dbw-egress fail until an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway is added, even though 0.0.0.0/0 goes to the firewall.

concepts.definition: The DNS behaviour in which a linked privatelink zone answers NXDOMAIN for another party's resource that has private endpoints, unless fallback or extra records are configured.
concepts.example: Linking privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net broke resolution for a supplier's storage account that had its own private endpoint.

questions.prompt: A Cinderline admin who holds Owner on the whole subscription tries to add an outbound rule to the network security group inside rg-dbw-prod-managed, and Azure refuses. What refused the change?

options.text: A system deny assignment on the managed resource group, which applies even though the Owner role grants the action.
options.rationale: Deny assignments are created and managed by Azure and block actions that a role assignment would allow; Databricks protects its managed group this way.

options.text: Unity Catalog, because network changes need the metastore admin role.
options.rationale: Unity Catalog governs data objects in the Databricks account; it takes no part in Azure management operations on a network security group.

options.text: The storage account firewall, because the managed group contains the workspace storage account.
options.rationale: A storage firewall filters data requests to one storage account's endpoint; it cannot refuse a management edit to a network security group.

options.text: A missing Storage Blob Data Contributor role at subscription scope.
options.rationale: Data roles authorize reading and writing blobs; they neither grant nor block management operations on network resources.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's Databricks account uses only the SCIM provisioning connector, and the nightly job must run as the Entra application sp-job-nightly. What will an admin find in the account?

options.text: sp-job-nightly is missing: the SCIM connector does not sync Entra service principals, so it is added another way or the account moves to automatic identity management.
options.rationale: Documented: SCIM provisioning cannot sync Microsoft Entra ID service principals or nested groups, and automatic identity management can.

options.text: sp-job-nightly is present, because every Entra object in the tenant is synced.
options.rationale: SCIM syncs the users and groups assigned to the connector, and service principals are an explicit documented gap.

options.text: sp-job-nightly is present, but only as a member of grp-quality-analysts.
options.rationale: Group membership does not carry a service principal through SCIM; the connector does not sync service principals at all.

options.text: The job can run as the access connector's managed identity instead.
options.rationale: The managed identity is a storage identity used by Unity Catalog, not a Databricks principal that a job runs as.

questions.prompt: On a VNet-injected classic cluster with secure cluster connectivity, which statement about the control path is accurate?

options.text: The cluster opens an outbound connection on port 443 to the relay, and administration requests return through it; no inbound port is opened.
options.rationale: Documented: nodes have no public IP, the VNet has no open ports, and each cluster initiates the relay connection.

options.text: The control plane connects inbound to each node's public IP on a management port.
options.rationale: With secure cluster connectivity nodes have no public IP address and the VNet opens no inbound port.

options.text: The analyst's browser sends commands straight to the cluster over the transit VNet.
options.rationale: The browser talks to the workspace in the control plane; commands reach clusters only through the relay tunnel.

options.text: Control traffic travels through the storage account's private endpoint.
options.rationale: A storage private endpoint carries the storage path; the control path goes to the relay, or through back-end Private Link if it is configured.

questions.prompt: Security requires every packet leaving classic compute to pass Cinderline's Azure Firewall. Which setup can meet that requirement?

options.text: VNet injection with a route table on both workspace subnets sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall, plus allow rules for the destinations Databricks needs.
options.rationale: Only the injected pattern lets Cinderline attach route tables; the firewall then needs allow rules for the required destinations.

options.text: The default managed VNet with an outbound deny rule added to its network security group.
options.rationale: The default VNet and its NSG sit in the locked managed resource group, and the deny assignment refuses the edit.

options.text: A network connectivity configuration attached to the workspace.
options.rationale: An NCC governs serverless compute in the Databricks account, not classic nodes in a VNet.

options.text: Front-end Private Link with the browser_authentication endpoint.
options.rationale: Front-end Private Link secures users' inbound connections to the workspace; it does not route compute egress.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's injected workspace uses a /26 host subnet and a /26 container subnet. Two clusters of 20 nodes each are running. How many more nodes can start before addresses run out?

options.rationale: Each /26 has 64 addresses minus 5 reserved, so 59 usable; each node takes one in each subnet, the workspace caps at 59, and 40 are in use.
Subtracting 40 from 64 ignores the five addresses Azure reserves in every subnet.
Adding the two subnets into one pool is the error: a node needs an address in each, so each subnet caps the workspace separately at 59.

options.text: None, because each running cluster holds a whole subnet.
options.rationale: Clusters share both subnets; addresses are consumed per node, not per cluster.

questions.prompt: With the route table in the first state, a notebook on the cluster downloads a package from a public repository. Which next hop carries the connection first?

options.text: The firewall at 10.10.0.4, because only the 0.0.0.0/0 route contains that public address.
options.rationale: Longest prefix match finds no more specific route for an arbitrary public address, so the default route to the virtual appliance applies.

options.text: The Internet next hop, because the AzureDatabricks route allows outbound traffic.
options.rationale: A service-tag route covers only the prefixes in that tag; other destinations do not match it.

options.text: The virtual network, because the 10.20.0.0/22 route is the most specific.
options.rationale: A route applies only when the destination falls inside its prefix, and a public repository is not inside the VNet range.

options.text: None: routes with service tags block every other destination.
options.rationale: Routes choose next hops; blocking is a firewall or NSG decision, or an explicit None next hop.

questions.prompt: Security sets AllowSharedKeyAccess to false on stcinderlinelake. Which legacy notebook still reads its files?

options.text: The one using OAuth 2.0 with the Entra service principal sp-legacy-etl.
options.rationale: Requests authorized with Microsoft Entra ID are unaffected when Shared Key is disallowed.

options.text: The one configured with the storage account key.
options.rationale: Shared Key is exactly what is disallowed; every request authorized with the account key is rejected.

options.text: The one using a service SAS that expires next month.
options.rationale: A service SAS is signed with the account key, so it is rejected once Shared Key is disallowed, whatever its expiry.

options.text: The one using an account SAS limited to read-only.
options.rationale: An account SAS is also authorized with Shared Key; narrowing its permissions does not change how it is authorized.

questions.prompt: From a cluster in the injected workspace, nslookup stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net returns a public address, while the private endpoint pe-lake-dfs shows Approved. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net is not linked to the cluster's VNet, and no DNS forwarding sends the query to a resolver that sees it.
options.rationale: Only a linked zone or a forwarding resolver turns the public CNAME into the endpoint's private address; the endpoint's own health cannot change the answer.

options.text: The access connector's managed identity lacks Storage Blob Data Reader.
options.rationale: A missing role produces a refusal from storage after a connection is made; it cannot change what DNS answers.

options.text: sp-job-nightly lacks SELECT on the table.
options.rationale: Unity Catalog privileges are checked before any storage request and have no influence on name resolution.

options.text: The host subnet's NSG lacks an inbound rule from the storage account.
options.rationale: Connections to storage are outbound from the node, and NSG rules do not change DNS answers.

questions.prompt: The nightly job fails with a 403 returned by stcinderlinelake, after SHOW GRANTS confirmed that sp-job-nightly holds SELECT. Which check comes next?

options.text: The role assignments of the storage credential's managed identity on stcinderlinelake, then the account's network rules.
options.rationale: The catalog agreed and storage refused, so the next evidence is the storage chain: the identity's data role, then the network rules that also refuse with a 403.

options.text: Grant sp-job-nightly Storage Blob Data Reader on the storage account.
options.rationale: The job does not read storage with its own identity; the credential's managed identity does, so this grant would not be used.

options.text: Link the privatelink.azuredatabricks.net zone to the workspace VNet.
options.rationale: The 403 came from the storage account, so the request reached it; DNS for the workspace URL is not in question.

options.text: Grant sp-job-nightly ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog.
options.rationale: The catalog already agreed; a broader grant widens access without touching the layer that refused.

questions.prompt: A read from an injected cluster to stcinderlinelake times out with no error from any service. Which first step gives the most information?

options.text: Resolve stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net from the cluster itself and compare the answer with the private endpoint's address.
options.rationale: The DNS answer on the asking network decides every later hop, and it takes one command to read.

options.text: Grant the access connector's identity Storage Blob Data Owner.
options.rationale: A timeout means no service refused anything; a broader role cannot make packets arrive.

options.text: Add an inbound allow rule from the internet to the host subnet's NSG.
options.rationale: Connections to storage are outbound from the cluster; an inbound rule adds exposure and fixes nothing.

options.text: Resolve the name from an administrator's laptop on the office network.
options.rationale: The laptop may use different DNS; only the asking network's answer shows what the cluster saw.

selfQuestions.prompt: A new ADLS Gen2 account, stcinderlinesup, must be governed by Unity Catalog. List, in order, the Azure and Databricks objects you would create or change, and say who at Cinderline owns each step.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Azure, by the cloud and storage team: confirm hierarchical namespace is enabled; decide whether ac-cinderline-uc is reused or a new access connector is created; assign its managed identity Storage Blob Data Reader or Contributor at container scope; admit it through the account's network rules or a private endpoint. Databricks, by a metastore admin or a holder of the create privileges: a storage credential naming the connector's resource ID, an external location for the abfss path, then grants to groups on the location and tables. Finally, test a read as a non-admin principal.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The order follows dependencies: nothing in Unity Catalog works until the Azure role exists, and grants come last so access is never wider than intended. Reusing one connector for several accounts is acceptable when one identity owning both is intended.

selfQuestions.prompt: The nightly job fails with PERMISSION_DENIED on SELECT. A colleague proposes giving sp-job-nightly Storage Blob Data Reader on stcinderlinelake. Explain why that does not fix the failure, what it would change, and what you would do instead.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The refusal came from Unity Catalog's application chain, so no storage request was made and no Azure role was consulted; a storage role for the job's service principal changes nothing about that refusal. It would, however, let sp-job-nightly read the files directly with its own Entra token, outside Unity Catalog's privileges. Instead, grant SELECT on the table, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA if missing, to sp-job-nightly or its group, and rerun as that principal.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The fix goes to the layer that refused, and the smallest grant restores the job without widening access; granting the privilege to a group the job belongs to is an acceptable alternative.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline moves the nightly query to a serverless SQL warehouse. stcinderlinelake currently admits only the injected VNet's subnets, and the query fails. Describe two ways to admit serverless, what each requires and which team acts.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: First way: attach an NCC to the workspace and add the NCC's stable subnets to the storage account's virtual network rules; the storage owner acts, and public network access stays enabled but restricted. Second way: an account admin adds a private endpoint rule for the account's dfs sub-resource in the NCC, the storage owner approves the endpoint request in Azure, and after the rule reads ESTABLISHED and the change propagates the query is retested. The second also works with public network access disabled.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Both keep serverless out of Cinderline's VNet and change only what the storage account admits; the private endpoint suits a no-public-access policy but adds an approval step, and its networking charges are checked against current pricing. The managed identity's data role is unchanged either way.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the evidence rows you would attach to the ticket after fixing the denied case, and say for each what it does not prove.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Error row: the fictional PERMISSION_DENIED text, its time and the answering service, Unity Catalog; it proves nothing about storage. Principal row: the job's run-as identity, sp-job-nightly; it does not prove its grants. Grant row: SHOW GRANTS on the table before and after, showing SELECT added; it does not prove the connector's role or network rules. Rerun row: the successful run as sp-job-nightly with its time; it does not prove any other principal's access.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague reuses the AWS runbook on Azure by replacing 'IAM role' with 'service principal' and 'security group' with 'NSG'. Name three places where that translation produces a wrong step on Azure, and give the correct step for each.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Storage identity: Unity Catalog on Azure uses the access connector's managed identity, so the step is to check its data role assignment on the storage account, not to create or edit a service principal or a trust policy. Network rules: the NSG rules Databricks needs are managed through subnet delegation and must not be edited; egress changes go into route tables and the firewall. Private connectivity: an Azure Private Link fix usually means linking the Private DNS zone to the asking VNet or approving the endpoint, which the AWS runbook's endpoint steps do not cover.

beats.title: A classic workspace resource comes with a resource group you cannot edit
beats.outcome: Place the tenant, subscription, workspace resource, managed resource group and workspace storage, and say which of them Cinderline can change.
beats.explanation: On Azure, Cinderline's classic workspace is a resource, Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces, in a resource group of its subscription under its Entra tenant. Creating a classic workspace provisions a second, [[dbxfe-azure-resources-concept|managed resource group]] holding the workspace storage account, networking components and, while clusters run, their virtual machines. Azure protects that group with a system deny assignment, so even a subscription Owner cannot edit what is inside. Notice in the second state that the tag edit fails in the managed group and succeeds on the workspace resource, while the control plane stays in the Databricks account throughout.

Par bonnet ke andar ka engine company ki seal mein hai; maalik bhi khole toh seal mana karti hai. Engine Cinderline ki sadak par chalta hai, lekin uski wiring sirf company chhedti hai.
samajh.mapping: The car is the workspace resource Cinderline owns and tags, the sealed engine bay is the managed resource group, and the seal is the system deny assignment that even a subscription Owner cannot break.
