handbook.markdown:
The workspace resource, type `Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces`, lives in a resource group Cinderline chooses, in a subscription that trusts one Microsoft Entra tenant. Creating a classic workspace through the portal, Azure CLI, PowerShell, Bicep or an ARM template also provisions a managed resource group holding the resources the workspace needs: virtual machines, storage accounts and networking components; the Microsoft.Databricks API's Serverless compute mode does not accept a managed resource group. The creating user becomes a workspace admin; creation takes minutes and occasionally hours.

The managed group is protected by a system deny assignment. Azure RBAC defines deny assignments as blocks on specific actions that apply even when a role assignment grants them, created and managed by Azure rather than by customers. Community answers on Microsoft Q&A describe the Databricks case: Owners cannot change tags or settings inside the managed group, the assignment disappears only when the workspace is deleted, and tags go on the workspace resource. Treat the group as read-only evidence.

| Object | Where it lives | Who changes it |
|---|---|---|
| `dbw-cinderline-prod` | `rg-cinderline-data` | Cinderline |
| Workspace storage account | managed group | Databricks, through the workspace |
| Default VNet, NSG, NAT gateway | managed group | Databricks |
| Control plane, web application | Databricks account | Databricks |

The workspace storage account holds workspace system data and the DBFS root; Cinderline's governed tables live in its own ADLS Gen2 account. To inspect without changing anything:

```powershell
Get-AzDenyAssignment -ResourceGroupName rg-dbw-prod-managed
```

or open the group's Access control (IAM) page and its Deny assignments tab. A refused edit there is expected behaviour, not a missing role, and no broader role overrides it. Nothing here creates a workspace.

beats.recap: The workspace resource is Cinderline's to tag and configure; the managed resource group beside it is locked by a system deny assignment.
beats.changeNote: The title, explanation and handbook now say the managed resource group comes with a classic workspace, not with every workspace. Source: the Microsoft.Databricks REST API specification (2026-01-01, pinned commit 2094b1c), where a Serverless-mode workspace takes no managed resource group.

beats.title: Entra issues every identity, and two systems authorize them separately
beats.outcome: Classify a user, group, service principal and managed identity by where each is created, how it reaches Databricks and which system grants it access.
beats.explanation: Every Cinderline identity starts in the Microsoft Entra tenant: analysts are users in groups, the nightly job is an application [[dbxfe-azure-entra-concept|service principal]], and the access connector carries a [[dbxfe-azure-managedid-concept|managed identity]] whose service principal has no application object and no secret anyone holds. Databricks learns users, groups and service principals through provisioning. Then two systems grant separately: Unity Catalog privileges inside Databricks, Azure role assignments on Azure resources. Notice in the table's second state that automatic identity management brings the nested group and the service principal that SCIM left behind.

handbook.markdown:
Microsoft Entra ID holds four kinds of identity that matter here. Users and groups are people and their teams. An application service principal is the tenant's instance of an application object and authenticates with credentials, such as a secret or certificate, that someone manages. A managed identity is a service principal Azure creates for a resource, with no application object and no credential anyone can read: a system-assigned identity lives and dies with its resource, a user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that several resources can share.

The Databricks account does not read the tenant directly; identities are provisioned. The SCIM provisioning connector syncs users and groups but, as documented, not nested groups and not Entra service principals. Automatic identity management syncs users, groups, memberships, nested groups and service principals, and is documented as enabled by default for accounts created after 1 August 2025; read the account's actual setting instead of inferring it from a date. An Entra Global Administrator establishes the first account admin, after which account admins run the account console, which opens in the user's default tenant.

After provisioning, two authorities act on the same Entra identities:

| Identity | Databricks side | Azure side |
|---|---|---|
| Analyst in `grp-quality-analysts` | Unity Catalog privileges through the group | None needed for queries |
| `sp-job-nightly` | Run-as principal of the job, with its own grants | None needed for queries |
| `ac-cinderline-uc` identity | Not a Databricks principal | Data role on `stcinderlinelake` |

A Unity Catalog grant never creates an Azure role assignment, and an Azure role never creates a Unity Catalog privilege. When a job fails, first establish which identity acted: a job runs as its run-as principal, not as the person who wrote it.

beats.recap: One tenant issues every identity, but a Unity Catalog grant and an Azure role assignment are separate permissions held in separate systems.
beats.changeNote: The identity table no longer says a managed identity can never be a Databricks principal; it says the connector's identity is not provisioned in this design. Source: the Databricks Terraform provider documentation (docs/index.md, pinned commit b1d7b85), where a managed identity added to a workspace as a service principal works.

beats.title: One query crosses four paths, and Entra signs the first
beats.outcome: Trace a query's author, control, execution and storage paths on Azure and name the control at each boundary.
beats.explanation: When an analyst runs a query, four [[dbxfe-azure-paths-concept|paths]] carry it. The author path runs from the browser to the workspace URL after an Entra sign-in. The control path runs from the control plane to compute; classic nodes reach it by dialling out to the secure cluster connectivity relay. The execution path is the cluster or serverless warehouse running the query once Unity Catalog agrees. The storage path runs from compute to an abfss address. Notice in the serverless state that the control, execution and storage paths never enter Cinderline's VNet.

handbook.markdown:
Follow one query from an analyst's browser to the lake and name the owner of every hop.

| Path | Hop | Control | Fails as |
|---|---|---|---|
| Author | Browser, Entra sign-in, workspace URL | Entra authentication; front-end Private Link if enabled | Sign-in error, or a private-network validation error |
| Control | Control plane, relay, classic node | Secure cluster connectivity: the node dials out on 443 | Cluster never reaches running |
| Execution | Cluster or serverless warehouse runs the plan | Unity Catalog privileges of the acting principal | PERMISSION_DENIED |
| Storage | Compute to an `abfss://` address | Credential's managed identity, data role, storage network rules, DNS, routes | 403 from storage, or a timeout |

On an injected classic cluster, the node sits in `vnet-cinderline-data` with no public IP. It opens the control-path connection itself, to a relay address that differs from the web application's, so no inbound rule is ever involved. The storage path leaves from the same subnet and obeys its route table, NSG and DNS.

On a serverless warehouse, execution moves into the Databricks account, inside a network boundary for the workspace. Cinderline's subnets, routes and firewall leave the control, execution and storage paths; the storage path is governed by the network connectivity configuration attached to the workspace and by the storage account's own rules.

What stays identical is the order: authentication before authorization, the catalog before storage. That order is what makes a denied request readable, because the first layer that says no is the layer to fix. One box labelled Databricks cannot show any of this, which is why the four paths are drawn separately.

beats.recap: Author, control, execution and storage paths each cross a different boundary, and serverless removes Cinderline's VNet from three of them.

beats.title: Two supported patterns hand Cinderline different network duties
beats.outcome: Compare the default managed VNet with VNet injection by who creates, changes and diagnoses each network piece.
beats.explanation: A classic workspace gets its network in one of two supported [[dbxfe-azure-patterns-concept|patterns]]. In the default pattern Databricks creates the virtual network, subnets, network security group and NAT gateway inside the locked managed resource group: little to operate, little to change. With VNet injection the network is Cinderline's own: its VNet, two delegated subnets, route tables, firewall, private endpoints and DNS, while Databricks still manages the security rules it needs. Notice in the third state that a firewall route, private endpoints and back-end Private Link exist only in the injected column.

samajh.text: Do tarah ke office socho. Co-working space mein building waale hi wiring, AC, gate aur internet chalate hain; tum desk use karte ho, badal kuch nahi sakte. Apne kiraye ke floor par wiring, gate aur internet tumhare hain, par lift ke rules building ke hi rehte hain. Pehle mein kam kaam aur kam control; doosre mein poora control, aur kuch toote toh pehla phone tumhare network waale ko jaata hai.
samajh.mapping: The co-working space is the default managed VNet in the locked group, the rented floor is the injected VNet Cinderline owns, and the building's lift rules are the NSG rules Databricks keeps through subnet delegation.
samajh.boundary: An office tenant can move floors at will; the network pattern is normally chosen when the workspace is created, and the control plane sits outside both buildings.

handbook.markdown:
Both patterns are supported; they differ in who operates the network and therefore who diagnoses it.

**Default managed VNet.** Databricks creates the VNet, subnets, NSG and a NAT gateway inside the locked managed resource group. Secure cluster connectivity is on for portal and ARM deployments, so nodes carry no public IP. Cinderline cannot add routes, NSG rules, private endpoints or custom DNS there. It fits when no network requirement goes beyond Azure's defaults.

**VNet injection.** Cinderline supplies a VNet (a /16 to /24 range) and two dedicated subnets delegated to `Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces`. Databricks still provisions and manages the NSG rules it needs through the delegation; Cinderline owns the rest: address planning, NAT gateway or firewall egress, user-defined routes, service or private endpoints, custom DNS, and back-end Private Link, which requires the Premium plan and injection.

A worked decision for Cinderline's second workspace:

| Requirement | Default | Injection |
|---|---|---|
| All egress inspected by the hub firewall | Not possible | UDR 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall |
| Storage reached only through private endpoints | Not possible | Endpoint in `snet-pe` plus DNS |
| Clusters reach the control plane privately | Not possible | Back-end Private Link, on Premium |
| Smallest operational load | Yes | No: addresses, routes and DNS to maintain |

The requirements pick injection, and with it a duty: launch timeouts are now Cinderline's to diagnose first. Serverless compute sits outside both patterns; its connectivity is configured through a network connectivity configuration. The documentation also has a page on updating an existing workspace's network configuration; read it before treating the choice as permanent, and never promise a migration without it. Nothing here provisions a network.

beats.recap: The default pattern trades control for simplicity; VNet injection gives Cinderline the routes, firewall, endpoints and DNS, and with them the diagnosis.

beats.title: VNet injection needs two delegated subnets and opens no inbound port
beats.outcome: Size and check the host and container subnets of an injected workspace, and explain why no inbound rule is needed.
beats.explanation: An injected workspace takes two dedicated subnets, host and container, each delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces and used by nothing else. Every cluster node takes one address in each, and Azure reserves five addresses per subnet, so subnet size caps the whole workspace. With [[dbxfe-azure-vnet-concept|secure cluster connectivity]] nodes get no public IP and the VNet opens no inbound port: each cluster dials out on port 443 to the relay. Notice in the second state that a /26 pair runs out at 59 nodes however many clusters share it.
beats.hint: Count addresses per subnet, not per workspace: each node needs one in both.

handbook.markdown:
An injected workspace's capacity is an address calculation, and its connectivity is outbound only.

Each node takes one address in the host subnet and one in the container subnet, and Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet. The documented minimum subnet size is /26 and the VNet range is /16 to /24; read the current page before designing:

| Subnet size | Addresses | Usable after 5 reserved | Maximum nodes |
|---|---|---|---|
| /26 | 64 | 59 | 59 |
| /25 | 128 | 123 | 123 |
| /24 | 256 | 251 | 251 |

The two subnets are separate pools, so the maximum is the usable count of either subnet, not their sum. Cinderline's peak of three 20-node clusters needs 60 nodes; a /26 pair holds 59, so one launch fails for want of an address, not because of a rule. Size for the peak plus autoscaling headroom.

Subnet delegation lets Databricks provision and manage the NSG rules the workspace needs; do not modify or delete them. The subnets are dedicated: no other workspace or Azure resource may use them, so private endpoints go into a separate subnet such as `snet-pe`.

With secure cluster connectivity both subnets are private: nodes have no public IP and the VNet opens no inbound port. Each cluster opens an outbound connection on port 443 to the relay, and administration requests travel back through it. A launch therefore depends on the outbound side: an egress method (Databricks recommends a NAT gateway on both subnets for a stable egress IP), a route, DNS resolution and outbound rules that allow the connection. Adding inbound rules never rescues a launch.

To inspect: free addresses per subnet, the delegation on both subnets, the NSG and NAT gateway associations and, when a firewall is in the path, its log for the relay address.

beats.recap: Two delegated subnets, one address per node in each, five reserved per subnet and outbound-only connectivity: size them for the peak node count.

beats.title: A route table decides where egress goes, and service tags name the destinations
beats.outcome: Predict the next hop for a cluster's outbound connection from a subnet route table that uses service tags.
beats.explanation: In an injected workspace, egress follows the route table on the two subnets, and Azure picks the longest matching prefix, so a specific route beats the default. Cinderline sends 0.0.0.0/0 to its firewall as a virtual appliance and adds [[dbxfe-azure-udr-concept|user-defined routes]] with service tags for what Databricks needs: AzureDatabricks for the control plane, relay and web application, Storage for artifact and log storage, EventHub for logging. Notice in the second state that deleting the AzureDatabricks route sends relay traffic to a firewall with no matching rule, and launches stop.
beats.hint: Find the most specific prefix that contains the destination address.

handbook.markdown:
Every subnet has system routes; a route table associated with the subnet adds user-defined routes that override them. For each outbound packet Azure picks the route with the longest matching prefix, so a /22 VNet route beats a 0.0.0.0/0 default, and a service-tag route beats the default for addresses in that tag.

Cinderline's route table `rt-dbw-egress`, attached to both workspace subnets:

```bash
az network route-table route create \
  --resource-group rg-cinderline-net --route-table-name rt-dbw-egress \
  --name default-to-firewall --address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --next-hop-type VirtualAppliance --next-hop-ip-address 10.10.0.4

az network route-table route create \
  --resource-group rg-cinderline-net --route-table-name rt-dbw-egress \
  --name to-azuredatabricks --address-prefix AzureDatabricks \
  --next-hop-type Internet
```

The Databricks page asks for a route for every type of outbound connection and recommends service tags over IP addresses: `AzureDatabricks` for the control plane, relay and web application, `Storage` for artifact and log storage, `EventHub` for logging. Internet-bound traffic to Azure services travels the Azure backbone. A route table holds a limited number of service-tag routes (25 at the time of writing), and an explicit prefix wins over a tag on an exact match.

Routing everything through the firewall instead is legitimate, but then the firewall must allow each required destination, and that allowlist is Cinderline's to maintain as addresses change. The deletion in the visual shows the failure shape: relay traffic falls to the default route, the firewall has no rule, packets are dropped, and clusters stop launching with no refusal anywhere.

VNets created with API versions released after 31 March 2026 get private subnets by default, and in a private subnet a route with next hop Internet, such as the service-tag routes above, fails unless an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway is also configured: the route to the firewall does not carry that traffic. Azure's page also says private subnets do not apply to delegated subnets hosting PaaS services, whose outbound connectivity the service manages, so read each workspace subnet's setting rather than assuming, and plan an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway on both subnets from the first day. Where your permissions allow, inspect the effective routes of a node's network interface, not only the route table.

beats.recap: Longest prefix wins: service-tag routes keep Databricks' destinations reachable, and everything else follows the default route to the firewall.
beats.changeNote: The default-outbound paragraph now says that in a private subnet the Internet-next-hop service-tag routes also need an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway, since the firewall route does not carry them, and notes Azure's exception for delegated subnets. Source: Microsoft's Default Outbound Access page source (azure-docs, pinned commit 194fd50).

beats.title: Account keys and SAS tokens authorize whoever holds them
beats.outcome: Contrast Shared Key, SAS and service-principal secrets with a Unity Catalog credential, and predict which keep working when Shared Key is disallowed.
beats.explanation: Before Unity Catalog, notebooks reached ADLS Gen2 by putting a secret into the Spark configuration: a storage account key, a SAS token or an Entra service principal's client secret. A [[dbxfe-azure-sharedkey-concept|Shared Key]] opens every resource in the account; service and account SAS tokens are signed with that key; the storage account sees the key, not the person who ran the cell. Notice in the second state that disallowing Shared Key breaks the key and both key-signed SAS kinds, while the Entra-authorized methods keep working.

samajh.text: Society ke main gate ki ek master chaabi hai: jiske haath lage, woh har flat khol sakta hai, aur guard ko pata hi nahi chalta kaun andar aaya. SAS token usi chaabi se banayi hui ek parchi hai: limited, time-bound, par jo le jaaye usi ki. Managed identity waala tareeka alag hai: guard har aane waale ka ID card dekhta hai aur list se milata hai ki usko kahan jaane ki ijaazat hai.
samajh.mapping: The master key is the storage account key, the chit is a SAS signed with that key, and the ID-card check against a list is Entra authorization of a named identity against an Azure role assignment.
samajh.boundary: A SAS carries its own permissions, scope and expiry, and a user delegation SAS is signed through Entra rather than with the account key, so not every token is a copy of the master key.

handbook.markdown:
Before Unity Catalog, a notebook or cluster reached ADLS Gen2 directly with the ABFS driver and a secret in its configuration. The contrast matters because such configurations survive in old jobs.

```python
# Legacy pattern, shown only as contrast: a storage account key in the Spark configuration
spark.conf.set(
    "fs.azure.account.key.stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net",
    dbutils.secrets.get(scope="legacy", key="lake-account-key"),
)
spark.read.format("delta").load(
    "abfss://quality@stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net/accepted/inspections"
)
```

| Method | Authorized by | Who can use it | Survives Shared Key disallowed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Account key | Shared Key | Anyone holding the key, whole account | No |
| Service or account SAS | Signed with the account key | Anyone holding the token, within its scope | No |
| User delegation SAS | Microsoft Entra ID | Anyone holding the token, signed through Entra | Yes |
| Service principal OAuth | Microsoft Entra ID | The service principal; its secret must be guarded | Yes |

A Shared Key grants access to every resource in the account, and a SAS signed with it inherits the problem; SAS generation cannot even be audited. Setting `AllowSharedKeyAccess` to false makes Azure Storage reject key-authorized requests while Entra-authorized ones continue; other services that depend on Shared Key are checked first.

Two consequences for diagnosis. A legacy read that fails right after a security change may be a Shared Key refusal, not a Unity Catalog problem. And a legacy secret can hide a broken Unity Catalog chain: an external location with fallback mode enabled falls back to cluster credentials when Unity Catalog's are not sufficient, so record whether fallback is on during a migration. The target state has no key, SAS or client secret in any configuration; the Unity Catalog credential in the next beat replaces them.

beats.recap: A key or key-signed SAS authorizes the bearer and names no person; Entra-authorized access names an identity and survives Shared Key being disallowed.

beats.title: Unity Catalog reaches ADLS through an access connector's managed identity
beats.outcome: Assemble the chain from access connector to external table and name the Azure or Databricks object at each link.
beats.explanation: Unity Catalog replaces the secret with an [[dbxfe-azure-connector-concept|access connector]]: an Azure resource, Microsoft.Databricks/accessConnectors, carrying a system-assigned managed identity. Cinderline grants that identity a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor on stcinderlinelake, registers the connector's resource ID as a storage credential, and binds an external location to [[dbxfe-azure-abfss-concept|abfss://quality@stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net/accepted]]. No secret exists to leak or rotate. Notice in the second state that removing the role assignment leaves every Unity Catalog object intact, yet reads fail at storage.

handbook.markdown:
The Unity Catalog chain on Azure has five links, and the one that authorizes reads in Azure is a role assignment on the storage account. Databricks' Terraform guide also gives the connector's identity Storage Account Contributor, Storage Queue Data Contributor and EventGrid EventSubscription Contributor beside the data role, so read all of its role assignments.

1. **Access connector** `ac-cinderline-uc`, type `Microsoft.Databricks/accessConnectors`, in `rg-cinderline-data`, carrying a system-assigned managed identity; a user-assigned identity can be attached instead.
2. **Role assignment**: the identity holds a data role, Storage Blob Data Contributor for read-write or Storage Blob Data Reader for read-only, scoped to the account or a container. Role changes can take up to ten minutes to apply.
3. **Storage credential** `cinderline_lake_cred`, which names the connector's resource ID:

```python
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from databricks.sdk.service.catalog import AzureManagedIdentityRequest

w = WorkspaceClient()
w.storage_credentials.create(
    name="cinderline_lake_cred",
    azure_managed_identity=AzureManagedIdentityRequest(
        access_connector_id=(
            "/subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/rg-cinderline-data"
            "/providers/Microsoft.Databricks/accessConnectors/ac-cinderline-uc"
        )
    ),
)
```

4. **External location**, which binds a path to the credential:

```sql
CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION IF NOT EXISTS cinderline_quality
  URL 'abfss://quality@stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net/accepted'
  WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL cinderline_lake_cred);
```

5. **External table** `quality.accepted.inspections` under that path, with privileges granted to groups.

Creating the credential needs metastore admin or the CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL privilege; creating the location needs CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the metastore and the credential. A managed identity needs no secret rotation and, unlike a service principal, lets Unity Catalog reach storage protected by network rules. Unity Catalog checks the caller's access to the credential or location before it authenticates to Azure at all.

The failure in the visual is common after a cleanup: the role assignment disappears, every Unity Catalog object still looks correct, and reads fail with a 403 from storage. Read the identity's role assignments on the account before touching any grant.

beats.recap: Connector, managed identity, Azure data role, storage credential, external location: the data role assignment is the Azure permission that authorizes the reads.
beats.changeNote: The chain no longer calls the data role the connector identity's only Azure permission; it names it as the role that authorizes reads. Source: the Databricks Terraform provider guide for Unity Catalog on Azure (pinned commit b1d7b85), which assigns the identity four roles.

beats.title: Application access and storage access are separate chains
beats.outcome: Separate who may query a table from what may read its files, and choose the right place to fix a refusal.
beats.explanation: Two chains meet at every read. [[dbxfe-azure-separation-concept|Application access]] asks whether an Entra-authenticated principal may use the workspace and holds USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT; Unity Catalog answers. Storage access asks whether the storage credential's managed identity holds a data role and whether the account's [[dbxfe-azure-netrules-concept|network rules]] admit it; Azure answers. Analysts need no Azure role on the lake, and the managed identity needs no Unity Catalog grant. Notice in the second state that a storage role for analysts opens a path around Unity Catalog.

samajh.text: Hospital socho. Doctor ko ward mein jaane ke liye hospital ka badge chahiye; dawai store se dawai laane ka kaam pharmacy runner karta hai, jiske paas store ki chaabi hai. Doctor ke badge mein gadbad ho toh runner ko nayi chaabi dene se kuch nahi sudhrega. Aur doctor ko khud store ki chaabi de do, toh woh ward ke hisaab-kitaab ke bina seedha dawai utha sakta hai.
samajh.mapping: The ward badge is the analyst's Unity Catalog privilege, the pharmacy runner is the access connector's managed identity, and the store key is its Azure data role on the storage account.
samajh.boundary: A runner acts on a doctor's instruction at any time; the managed identity acts only inside requests Unity Catalog has already authorized, never on its own initiative.

handbook.markdown:
Every read of `quality.accepted.inspections` passes two chains that answer different questions.

**Application access** asks whether this principal may do this in Databricks. The analyst authenticates with Entra, is a user of the workspace, and holds `USE CATALOG` on `quality`, `USE SCHEMA` on `quality.accepted` and `SELECT` on the table, usually through `grp-quality-analysts`. Unity Catalog answers, and a no arrives as PERMISSION_DENIED before any storage request is made.

**Storage access** asks whether Databricks may reach the files. After Unity Catalog agrees, the read uses the storage credential's managed identity: Azure checks its data role on `stcinderlinelake` and the account's network rules. Both must pass; a resource instance rule, for example, admits the connector to the endpoint but grants no data access by itself.

```sql
SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE quality.accepted.inspections;
```

```bash
az role assignment list --assignee <managed-identity-principal-id> \
  --scope /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/rg-cinderline-data/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stcinderlinelake
```

The first proves the application chain and nothing about storage; the second proves the storage chain's role and nothing about network rules or grants.

The tempting wrong fix is a storage role for people. Granting analysts Storage Blob Data Reader does not repair a catalog refusal, because Unity Catalog still refuses, and it opens a second path: with their own Entra tokens they can read the files from any network the account admits, outside Unity Catalog's privileges and its record of Databricks queries. Keep data roles on managed identities and privileges on groups. Creating a storage account grants nobody data access through Entra, not even its creator; a role is always assigned explicitly.

beats.recap: Unity Catalog decides what a principal may query; the credential's managed identity, its Azure role and the network rules decide whether the files can be read.

beats.title: Serverless reaches Cinderline's resources through an NCC, not a subnet
beats.outcome: Explain how a network connectivity configuration gives serverless compute stable subnets or approved private endpoints to Cinderline's Azure resources.
beats.explanation: Serverless compute runs in the Databricks account, so Cinderline's route tables and firewall never see it. Instead an account admin attaches a [[dbxfe-azure-ncc-concept|network connectivity configuration]], a regional account object, to the workspace. Without further rules, serverless reaches Azure storage through service endpoints from stable subnets that Cinderline can admit in its storage network rules. A private endpoint rule makes Databricks request an endpoint on a resource, which the resource owner must approve. Notice in the second state that the rule sits PENDING, unusable, until approval.

handbook.markdown:
Serverless compute runs in the Databricks account, so Cinderline's subnets, route tables, NSGs and firewall are not on its path. Its reach into Cinderline's Azure resources is configured through a network connectivity configuration (NCC): an account-level, regional object that an account admin creates in the account console and attaches to workspaces in the same region.

Two ways in, both configured rather than built:

| Way in | How it works | Cinderline's step |
|---|---|---|
| Stable subnets | Serverless reaches Azure storage through service endpoints from subnets the NCC lists | Admit those subnets in the storage account's network rules |
| Private endpoint rule | Databricks requests a private endpoint on the resource, for a sub-resource such as `dfs` | The resource owner approves the request in Azure |

A rule's state says where it stands: PENDING until the owner approves, ESTABLISHED when usable, REJECTED or DISCONNECTED when the owner refused or removed it, and EXPIRED when nobody approved it within 14 days. Rules take effect only when ESTABLISHED, and most changes propagate within ten minutes but can take up to 24 hours, so a test straight after approval proves little. Reaching the workspace's root storage privately takes two endpoints, one for `blob` and one for `dfs`.

Private endpoint rules are documented for SQL warehouses, jobs, notebooks, Lakeflow pipelines and model serving endpoints. Without a rule, other resources see serverless connections arrive from NAT IPs. The documentation also describes a private network gateway that reaches a customer VNet through one delegated subnet; treat its availability as something to verify. Per-region limits on NCCs and endpoints exist; check current pricing for networking charges and read the current page before promising a design. Restricting where serverless may connect outbound is a separate control, a network policy, covered in the extension cards.

beats.recap: Serverless swaps Cinderline's subnet for an NCC: stable subnets to admit, or private endpoints that the resource owner must approve.

beats.title: A private endpoint works only when DNS returns its address
beats.outcome: Match each Private Link connection to its endpoint, network and Private DNS zone, and verify resolution before blaming a firewall.
beats.explanation: Azure Databricks has three [[dbxfe-azure-privatelink-concept|Private Link]] connections, enabled independently: front-end from users through databricks_ui_api and browser_authentication endpoints in a transit VNet, back-end from injected clusters through a databricks_ui_api endpoint, and outbound from serverless through the NCC. Storage takes one endpoint per sub-resource, dfs for abfss. Each works only when the name resolves to the endpoint's private address, through a [[dbxfe-azure-privatedns-concept|Private DNS zone]] linked to the asking VNet. Notice in the second state that without the link the same name returns a public address.

samajh.text: College campus mein library ka naya andar wala darwaza khula hai, par campus map ab bhi bahar ke main gate ka raasta dikhata hai. Students map dekh kar ghoom ke main gate pahunchte hain, jo ab band hai. Darwaza bilkul theek hai; bas map purana hai. Aur naya map har hostel ke notice board par alag se lagana padega, warna us hostel ke students purane raaste hi jaayenge.
samajh.mapping: The inner library door is the private endpoint, the campus map is DNS answered through a Private DNS zone, and each hostel's notice board is a VNet that must be linked to that zone.
samajh.boundary: A campus map is public to everyone, while a Private DNS zone answers only linked networks or resolvers that forward to it, and the endpoint must also be Approved before anyone can use it.

beats.hint: Ask what the name resolves to from the cluster itself, before anything else.

handbook.markdown:
Three Private Link connection types exist for Azure Databricks, each enabled independently, beside the endpoints Cinderline creates for its own storage:

| Connection | From | Endpoint sub-resource | Private DNS zone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Front-end (inbound) | Users' transit VNet | `databricks_ui_api`, `browser_authentication` | `privatelink.azuredatabricks.net` |
| Back-end (classic) | Injected workspace VNet | `databricks_ui_api` | `privatelink.azuredatabricks.net` |
| Serverless (outbound) | Databricks account | NCC private endpoint rules | Handled through the NCC |
| Storage for classic | `snet-pe` in the workspace VNet | `dfs` for abfss, `blob` for blob | `privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net`, `privatelink.blob.core.windows.net` |

The `browser_authentication` endpoint carries single sign-on over the private connection; back-end Private Link requires the Premium plan and VNet injection.

Resolution is the part that fails quietly. Public DNS answers `stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net` with a CNAME into `stcinderlinelake.privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net`. A network whose DNS consults a linked Private DNS zone gets the endpoint's private address; any other network gets the public one. The zone must therefore be linked to every VNet that asks, or reached through DNS forwarding in a hub-and-spoke design. DNS resolution and access control are independent: a correct answer proves nothing about approval, and an account with public network access disabled refuses public connections whatever DNS says.

Check from the asking network. In a notebook attached to the cluster:

```python
import socket
socket.gethostbyname("stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net")  # expect 10.20.2.5, not a public address
```

Then, with the Azure CLI:

```bash
az network private-dns link vnet list -g rg-cinderline-net -z privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net -o table
az network private-endpoint-connection list --id <storage-account-resource-id> -o table
```

Only Approved endpoints carry traffic. A user who reaches a Private Link workspace from the wrong network can meet an error that the Databricks SDK raises as a permission denial, PrivateLinkValidationError, although the cause is the network: read the message before touching a grant.

beats.recap: Three Private Link connections and one rule: the asking network must resolve the name to the endpoint's private address, and the endpoint must be Approved.

beats.title: A denial names its layer, and three Azure layers can refuse
beats.outcome: Order the checks for a refused request: acting principal, Unity Catalog privileges, the credential's data role, then storage network rules.
beats.explanation: A refused request arrived somewhere and something said no, so read [[dbxfe-azure-denied-concept|which layer]] said it. PERMISSION_DENIED from Databricks names the Unity Catalog principal and privilege, and storage was never contacted. A 403 from the storage account after the catalog agreed points at the credential's managed identity: its data role, or the account's network rules, whose refusals are 403s too. Notice in the timeline that the job's failure stops at step three: the fix is one grant to sp-job-nightly, then a rerun as that same principal.
beats.hint: Which service wrote the error text?

handbook.markdown:
**Case.** The nightly job, run as the application service principal `sp-job-nightly` on a serverless SQL warehouse, reads `quality.accepted.inspections`, an external table under `cinderline_quality`, whose credential uses the managed identity of `ac-cinderline-uc`. Error texts are fictional.

**Classification.** A service answered, so this is an authorization failure, not name resolution or reachability; identity is settled once the acting principal is confirmed.

**Ordered sequence.**
1. Record the exact error and which service returned it. `PERMISSION_DENIED: sp-job-nightly lacks SELECT on quality.accepted.inspections` comes from Unity Catalog; a `403 from stcinderlinelake` comes from Azure Storage.
2. Confirm the acting principal: the job's run-as identity, not its author, and that it exists in the account (SCIM does not sync service principals).
3. Check `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` with `SHOW GRANTS`. A missing privilege ends the search: storage was never contacted.
4. If the catalog agreed and storage refused, read the role assignments of the credential's managed identity on the account or container.
5. If the role is present, read the account's network rules and public-access setting; a network-rule refusal is also a 403, so read the error details, not only the status.
6. Apply the smallest change at the refusing layer, allow up to ten minutes for a role assignment, and rerun as the same principal.
7. Write the evidence row: error, answering service, principal, change, rerun result.

**Evidence to collect.** Error text and time; run-as identity; `SHOW GRANTS` output; the managed identity's role assignments; the network rule configuration.

**Wrong fixes.** A storage role for `sp-job-nightly` (the job never reads storage with its own identity), ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog, or a DNS change. One Azure-specific trap: a user reaching a Private Link workspace from the wrong network gets an error the SDK raises as a permission denial; its message names the network, which makes it a reachability case.

beats.recap: Read which service refused: Unity Catalog names a principal and privilege, storage 403s point at the credential's role or network rules; fix that layer only and rerun as the same principal.

beats.title: A request that never arrived leaves no refusal to read
beats.outcome: Run an ordered reachability diagnosis from the asking network: DNS answer, zone links, endpoint state, route, NSG and firewall.
beats.explanation: When nothing answers there is no error text from a service to read, only a timeout on the caller's side. Work outward from the asking network through each [[dbxfe-azure-unreachable-concept|reachability layer]]: what the name resolved to, whether the Private DNS zone is linked, whether the endpoint is Approved, which route carries the packet, and what the NSG and firewall allow. Notice in the timeline that the cluster's DNS returned a public address, the route sent it to the firewall, and the firewall dropped it silently: linking the zone, not a grant, is the fix.

samajh.text: Socho aap dost ko call karte ho aur ghanti bas bajti rehti hai: na koi uthata hai, na 'call rejected' ki awaaz aati hai. Aise mein 'usne mana kar diya' maan lena galat hai. Pehle dekho aapne kaunsa number dial kiya, phir network hai ya nahi, phir kahin call chupchaap block to nahi ho rahi. Jawab aata toh padh lete; jawab nahi aaya, isliye raasta check karo.
samajh.mapping: The dialled number is the DNS answer on the asking network, the mobile network is the route, a silently blocked call is a firewall drop, and a spoken 'call rejected' message is the refusal a denied request would carry.
samajh.boundary: A phone network usually tells you something; many Azure layers drop traffic silently, yet a storage account with public access disabled does answer with a refusal, so first check whether anything answered at all.

beats.hint: No refusal means no service to question; start from the asking network.

handbook.markdown:
**Case.** An injected classic cluster in `snet-dbw-host` reads `abfss://quality@stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net/accepted`. The account has public network access disabled and a private endpoint `pe-lake-dfs` (sub-resource `dfs`, address 10.20.2.5) in `snet-pe`. The subnets' default route goes to the hub firewall at 10.10.0.4. Error texts are fictional.

**Classification.** Nothing answered, so this is name resolution or reachability, never authorization: no grant or role can make a packet arrive.

**Ordered sequence, walking outward from the asking network.**
1. Record the symptom: `connect timed out: stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net:443` after retries, with the time and the cluster.
2. Resolve the name from the cluster itself (`socket.gethostbyname` in a notebook, or `nslookup` from a VM in the same subnet). A public address means the private zone was not consulted.
3. Check the Private DNS zone's VNet links, or the DNS forwarding path in a hub-and-spoke design. Here the zone was linked to the hub only.
4. Check the endpoint's connection state: only Approved carries traffic.
5. Read the route table on the subnet, and a node's effective routes where your permissions allow: where does the answered address go?
6. Read the effective NSG rules and the firewall log for that address and time. A drop with no reply confirms the path.
7. Fix the first broken step, retest from the same subnet and record the result.

In the visual's second state the answer is private but the endpoint is Pending, because the storage owner never approved it: ask for approval, then retest.

**Evidence to collect.** The DNS answer from the cluster with time; zone links; endpoint state; the route table or effective routes; the firewall log line.

**Azure-specific trap.** A wrong DNS answer does not always time out. If a route to the public endpoint exists, the account with public access disabled refuses the connection instead, and that refusal can look like a permission problem. Read which service answered, and why, before choosing a sequence. Never add inbound rules or grants to fix a path.

beats.recap: No refusal means no service to question: resolve from the asking network first, then zone links, endpoint state, route, NSG and firewall, and retest from the same place.

beats.title: Evidence lives in Azure and Databricks objects you can name
beats.outcome: Assemble a permissions and network evidence checklist in which every row names its object and what it does not prove.
beats.explanation: A diagnosis ends in evidence another engineer can re-check. Each [[dbxfe-azure-evidence-concept|evidence row]] names the boundary, what to capture, which Azure or Databricks object holds it, and what it does not prove. A role assignment export proves a permission and nothing about a route; a name lookup on the cluster proves resolution and nothing about approval; SHOW GRANTS proves the catalog and nothing about storage. Notice in the second state that the network rows are captured from the asking network, never from an administrator's laptop.

handbook.markdown:
A diagnosis is finished when another engineer can re-check it without asking you. Each evidence row carries four fields: the boundary, what to capture, the object that holds it, and what it does not prove.

Rules that keep the checklist honest:
- **Capture from the asking network.** DNS answers, effective routes and firewall logs differ by network; a laptop's result proves nothing about a cluster's.
- **Timestamp every row.** Role assignments take up to ten minutes to apply and NCC rule changes up to 24 hours; a test without a time cannot be ordered against the change.
- **Name the object.** "Permissions look fine" is not evidence; a `SHOW GRANTS` output or a role assignment export with its scope is.
- **Write the limit.** Each row states what it cannot prove, which is what stops a permission fix being applied to a network fault.
- **Keep secrets out.** No keys, SAS tokens, client secrets or bearer tokens in the ticket; record names and resource IDs.

For Cinderline's unreachable case after the fix, the rows read:

| Boundary | Captured | Does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| DNS answer | Lookup on the cluster: 10.20.2.5, with time | Endpoint approval |
| Zone link | `privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net` linked to `vnet-cinderline-data` | Firewall behaviour |
| Endpoint | `pe-lake-dfs` Approved | That a data role exists |
| Retest | Read succeeded from the same subnet, with time | Serverless behaviour |

Keep an unknowns list beside the checklist: tier, regional availability of each feature, preview status, charges and anything nobody has confirmed in the portal. Permission rows and network rows never substitute for each other.

beats.recap: Every evidence row names its boundary, its object and its limit, and network rows are captured from the network that asked.

beats.title: Azure is not AWS with new names: the boundaries sit in different objects
beats.outcome: List what differs between Cinderline's Azure and AWS deployments and refuse the parity shortcuts that break a diagnosis.
beats.explanation: Translating AWS terms one for one hides where Azure's boundaries sit, so keep an explicit [[dbxfe-azure-awsdiff-concept|difference list]]. A classic workspace is itself an Azure resource with a locked managed group, not a configuration pointing at a customer account. Injected subnets are delegated to Databricks, which keeps the security rules it needs. Storage identity is an access connector's managed identity holding an Azure role, with no trust policy to write. Private Link adds a browser_authentication endpoint and Private DNS zone links. Notice in the table that tier names differ too: Premium on Azure where the AWS pages say Enterprise.

handbook.markdown:
The questions transfer between clouds; the answers do not. Use this list to stop an AWS runbook being translated term for term.

**What differs from AWS**
- **The workspace.** On Azure a classic workspace is a resource, `Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces`, with a managed resource group locked by a system deny assignment. The AWS module describes a workspace configuration naming Cinderline's VPC and bucket in its AWS account.
- **Classic networking.** VNet injection uses two delegated subnets, host and container, and Databricks provisions the NSG rules it needs through the delegation; do not delete them. The AWS module uses a customer-managed VPC with at least two subnets and a security group.
- **Storage identity.** A Unity Catalog storage credential on Azure names an access connector whose managed identity holds an Azure data role; no trust policy is written. On AWS the credential wraps an IAM role that lives in the bucket's account.
- **Legacy access.** Azure's legacy path is a key, SAS or client secret in Spark configuration; AWS's is an instance profile on the cluster's instances.
- **A network door on storage.** Azure storage network rules (virtual network, IP, resource instance, trusted service) refuse with a 403 independently of roles.
- **Private connectivity.** Azure adds a `browser_authentication` endpoint for single sign-on and depends on Private DNS zone links per VNet.
- **Keys and tiers.** Customer-managed keys on Azure come from Key Vault or Managed HSM and cover managed disks (classic compute only), managed services and the DBFS root. Back-end Private Link and serverless egress control need Premium on Azure; the AWS pages name Enterprise for egress control and for customer-managed keys.
- **Identity.** Entra ID is the native directory: a Global Administrator seeds the first account admin, and the provisioning method decides whether service principals and nested groups arrive.

**What transfers.** Two compute planes; four request paths; catalog before storage in the denied sequence; DNS before routes in the unreachable sequence; evidence rows that name the object and its limit.

A three-cloud comparison keeps these as separate sourced answers per cloud and marks anything unverified as unknown rather than copying another cloud's answer.

beats.recap: Same planes and the same diagnostic order, but different owners, identities, network objects and tier names: never translate a runbook word for word.
beats.changeNote: The explanation, handbook and comparison table now describe a classic workspace, not every workspace, as a resource with a locked managed resource group. Source: the Microsoft.Databricks REST API specification (2026-01-01, pinned commit 2094b1c), where a Serverless-mode workspace takes no managed resource group.

extensionCards.prompt: What changes for Databricks and other services when firewall support is enabled on a workspace storage account?
extensionCards.answer: Public network access to the workspace storage account is blocked; Databricks reaches it through an access connector associated with the workspace, serverless through service or private endpoints, and outside services only through private endpoints.
extensionCards.explanation: The workspace storage account sits in the managed resource group and holds workspace system data and the DBFS root, so Cinderline cannot put its own rules on it directly; this [[dbxfe-azure-extension-workspace-firewall-concept|documented option]] is the supported way. One setting deserves a second look: with trusted services allowed, any Azure Databricks access connector in the same tenant can reach the account, which is broader than one workspace. Enabling it is a change to plan with the network team, not a toggle to try in production.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Explains how the one storage account Cinderline cannot edit directly is still closed to public networks, and what that closes off.

extensionCards.prompt: Which control restricts where Azure Databricks serverless compute may connect outbound, and what must hold before using it?
extensionCards.answer: A serverless egress control network policy, managed by account admins at account level, on a workspace in the Premium tier and in a region where it is available.
extensionCards.explanation: Cinderline's firewall only sees traffic leaving its own subnets, so it cannot restrict serverless compute. A [[dbxfe-azure-extension-egress-policy-concept|network policy]] is attached at the account level, one per workspace at a time, and sets the network access mode, including a full-access mode. Most changes refresh within ten minutes, but switching access modes or enforcement can take up to 24 hours, so try it on a non-critical workspace first. Regional availability was not confirmed in this build and is checked before any promise.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Names the only documented place to restrict serverless egress, with the tier and availability checks it needs.

extensionCards.prompt: Why might clusters in a newly created injected VNet fail to reach public endpoints though no route or firewall blocks them?
extensionCards.answer: Subnets in VNets created with API versions released after March 31, 2026 are private by default, so virtual machines need an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway.
extensionCards.explanation: Azure changed how new virtual networks get [[dbxfe-azure-extension-default-outbound-concept|default outbound access]]: with API versions released after March 31, 2026 their subnets have defaultOutboundAccess set to false unless configured otherwise, and virtual machines in them cannot reach public endpoints without a NAT gateway, a route to a firewall or another explicit method. Existing VNets are unchanged, which is why two workspaces with identical route tables can behave differently. Azure also says private subnets do not apply to delegated subnets hosting PaaS services, whose outbound connectivity the service manages, so check each subnet's setting rather than assuming; Databricks' recommendation of a NAT gateway on both injected subnets gives explicit outbound either way.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Explains a new failure shape that looks like a routing fault but comes from when and how the VNet was created.

extensionCards.prompt: How can linking privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net to Cinderline's VNet break access to a supplier's storage account?
extensionCards.answer: If the supplier's account has its own private endpoints, Cinderline's linked zone holds no record for it and answers NXDOMAIN, unless fallback to internet or another DNS configuration is added.
extensionCards.explanation: Azure's documentation warns that a network using a Private DNS zone for a resource type resolves public resources of that type only when they have no private endpoint connections. Once Cinderline links the dfs zone, every dfs name whose CNAME points into the privatelink namespace is answered there, including the supplier's, whose account has its own private endpoints. With no matching record the zone answers NXDOMAIN, so the read fails before any connection. [[dbxfe-azure-extension-dns-fallback-concept|Fallback to internet]] on the virtual network link, or a deliberate record, restores resolution.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Shows how fixing Cinderline's own private DNS can silently break a partner's access, a common cross-organization surprise.

recap.title: One resource, two patterns, two chains
recap.markdown: **A workspace resource in Cinderline's subscription, a locked managed resource group beside it, and the control plane in the Databricks account.** The default managed VNet trades control for simplicity; VNet injection hands Cinderline delegated subnets, routes, firewall, private endpoints and DNS, and with them the diagnosis. Every read passes two chains: Unity Catalog privileges for the Entra principal, then the access connector's managed identity, its Azure data role and the storage network rules. A private endpoint works only when the asking network resolves to it and it is Approved. A denial names its layer; a timeout names none. **Transfer challenge:** redraw the responsibility table for a supplier's ADLS account in another subscription of the same tenant, read from a serverless warehouse, marking which rows need the supplier's approval and which features are still unknown.

appliedTask.title: Move the nightly job to serverless without keys
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline moves the nightly job from an injected classic cluster, which read stcinderlinelake with a storage account key in its Spark configuration, to a serverless SQL warehouse in the same workspace. Security will then disallow Shared Key and disable public network access on the account. List, in order, what must exist on the Azure side and the Databricks side for the job to read the table, which responsibilities leave Cinderline's VNet, and what you would mark unknown before the design review.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Databricks side: a storage credential naming access connector ac-cinderline-uc; an external location for abfss://quality@stcinderlinelake.dfs.core.windows.net/accepted; USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT for sp-job-nightly; an NCC attached to the workspace with a private endpoint rule for the account's dfs sub-resource; and no key left in any configuration. Azure side: the connector's managed identity holding a blob data role on the account or container, and the storage owner's approval of the endpoint request until the rule reads ESTABLISHED. Leaving the VNet: routes, NSG and the egress firewall no longer carry this job; the NCC and its approvals do. Unknown: endpoint support and limits in the region, networking charges, the workspace tier, propagation timing, and whether any other workload still uses the key.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer follows the request from identity through catalog and credential to storage, then reachability through the NCC, keeps the two authorization chains separate, and turns every conditional feature into a verification item rather than a promise.
